Peltola’s Alaska win gives Democrats 56 Senate seats and a buffer in Republican states ahead of the 2028 elections.
Democrat Mary Peltola has won the United States Senate seat in Alaska, unseating two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. It is the Democrats’ first US Senate win in the state in more than a decade.
As of early Wednesday, The Associated Press news agency’s count gave her 50.1 percent of first-choice votes against Sullivan’s 45.8 percent, with an estimated 99 percent of votes counted.
Clearing the 50 percent mark matters. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a candidate who wins a majority of first-choice votes is elected outright, with no further rounds of counting.
The vote has been closely watched, not just because it is the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections, but because of a Republican legal challenge to the election over the listing of two candidates with nearly the same name – Republican Dan Sullivan and independent Daniel Sullivan. The legal challenge was thrown out just days before the election.
The Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Dan Sullivan to divide Republican votes in the state – a practice known as “ ballot stacking “.
But on Tuesday, it was clear that even if the “official” Dan Sullivan had received all the votes of his namesake, he would not have gained enough to beat Peltola.
Peltola’s win brings Democratic control of the Senate to 56 seats, against the Republicans’ 44.
Peltola, a Yup’ik Alaskan, became the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress when she won a special election for the state’s sole House of Representatives seat in 2022. She served from September 2022 to January 2025, losing her re-election bid in 2024.
On the Senate campaign trail this year, she played down her Democratic label, which remains unpopular in the state, and focused on local issues such as energy jobs, border security and gun rights.
Scott Lucas, a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told Al Jazeera that Peltola is viewed as a “safe pair of hands”.
“Alaska is a very small population, with a very, very large landmass, so it’s very important that you try to build up, across that large landmass, ties and community ties,” he said. “Peltola was seen as someone who had represented Alaska’s interests very well.”
Lucas described her as “a pragmatist, very much in that centre line of Democratic politics”. “Not too provocative, doesn’t really play identity politics,” he said. “She didn’t play on the idea this is all about Native Americans, even though she happens to be a Native American.”
Sullivan, by contrast, “was tarnished because he was there on Trump’s ticket, as it were”, Lucas said, though “he was very much a local candidate”. “Had the Trump administration done a better job on the issues, then I suspect Sullivan holds his seat,” he added.
In late May, Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, entered the race. On June 15, the state elections division removed him from the ballot. It said he had chosen the name to cause confusion with the senator, and pointed to his use of a political consultant who had previously worked for Peltola.
The courts reversed that decision. A superior court judge ruled he was eligible, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling on June 29. The two candidates appeared on the ballot as “Daniel J Sullivan Jr”, with no party affiliation, and “Dan S Sullivan”, Republican and incumbent. The retired teacher finished in the top four of the August primary, earning a place on the November ballot.
Republicans claimed he was a decoy. The New York Times later reported that Peltola campaign staff and Democratic operatives had worked to get him to contest. At Trump’s urging, the Department of Justice (DoJ) sued to delay certification if Senator Sullivan lost and to separate ballots cast for his namesake. Federal Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on November 1. The DoJ said it would appeal.
Lucas said this kind of “ballot stacking” – backing a minor candidate to pull votes from a rival – is not uncommon, and both parties have engaged in it in the past. If the second Sullivan had taken 2 percent of the vote, he explained, he could have pushed the incumbent below the 50 percent mark and forced a ranked-choice count. “You drain enough support from the Republican that you give yourself a better chance of winning,” he said.
In the end, he said, “I don’t think it made that much of a difference.” AP’s count gave Daniel J Sullivan Jr 1.7 percent, and Peltola won more than 50 percent of the vote.
Peltola is the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since Sullivan unseated Mark Begich in 2014. Her win is not a deciding factor in which party controls the chamber – Democrats already had enough seats to control the Senate – but Lucas said it is “significant in a wider context”.
Alaska is the latest in a string of Republican strongholds to switch to Democrats.
On election night, Democrats flipped seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. Later-arriving counts then confirmed that Mississippi had flipped, electing its first Black senator in 150 years, and now Alaska has taken the tally to nine.
Texas went Democratic for the first time since 1988, and Kansas for the first time since 1932.
“Alaska was one of the seats that it was thought that the Democrats might win,” Lucas said. “So that in itself is not as surprising as, say, Mississippi, which is really, really surprising. South Carolina was quite a surprise as well. But still, it reaffirms the extent of this Democratic surge.”
Those wins also give Democrats a buffer. Senators serve six-year terms, with about one-third of the 100 seats contested every two years, so the seats won this month will not be on the ballot again until 2032. By holding seats in states they would not normally carry, Democrats can make it much harder for Republicans to retake the Senate in 2028.
Finally, the win brings Democrats closer to the magical two-thirds majority. They now hold 56 seats, which Lucas called “a pretty good majority when even the most optimistic analysts regarding the Democrats were looking at 53 seats at most”. They will still need Republican support on issues to secure the two-thirds majority needed to overturn a presidential veto in both chambers.
A two-thirds vote in the Senate is needed to convict an official in an impeachment trial. The more seats Democrats hold, the fewer Republicans they need to win over to reach that threshold. For now, Lucas said, “They cannot pass legislation because Trump can veto it. So they still have to try to work with Republicans if they want to get any legislation across.”
Lucas expects the new Democratic majorities to propose legislation and hold hearings on accountability, “whether that be with respect to AI and technology, whether it be with respect to the Epstein case”, or the wealth of Trump and his family, including through cryptocurrency. “Meanwhile, the Republicans are a fractured party,” he said.
In North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, Trump’s inner circle imposed candidates on the party, and all three were lost. Democrats, by contrast, “went for more organic candidates, and Mary Peltola was one of them”, Lucas said.
“Diversity has become a bad word with the Trump camp,” Lucas said. “It’s interesting that in this very diverse election, you have your first US Muslim senator, you have your first US openly gay man in the Senate, and you have two Native American women who have won: Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and then Peltola. In this case, it was the party with the diversity of candidates that did better.”

Nvidia , Çin pazarına yönelik stratejisinde önemli bir değişikliğe gidiyor. Şirketin geçici CEO'su Colette Kress , Nvidia'nın artık Çin'e lisanslı Hopper mimarili veri merkezi ürünleri göndermediğini açıkladı . Bu kapsamda şirketin H200 yapay zeka çiplerinin Çin'e sevkiyatı da sona ermiş oldu.
Karar, Nvidia'nın kurucu ortağı ve uzun yıllar CEO'luk görevini üstlenen Jensen Huang'ın geçen hafta görevinden ayrılmasının ardından gerçekleştirilen i lk finansal sonuç toplantısında açıklandı. Aynı gün Nvidia, ulusal güvenlik politikaları, ihracat kontrollerine uyum ve küresel ticaret risklerini takip edecek yönetim kurulu seviyesinde yeni bir komite kurduğunu da duyurdu .
Hatırlatmak gerekirse ABD Başkanı Donald Trump , geçtiğimiz yılın aralık ayında Nvidia'nın H200 çiplerini belirli Çinli müşterilere satmasına izin vermişti . Jensen Huang ve Trump yönetimi arasında şekillenen düzenleme kapsamında çiplerin ABD üzerinden gönderilmesi ve ABD hükümetinin satışlardan yüzde 25 oranında pay alması öngörülüyordu. H200, Nvidia'nın önceki nesil Hopper mimarisini temel almasına rağmen özellikle yapay zeka modellerinin eğitimi ve çalıştırılması açısından halen güçlü bir veri merkezi ürünü olarak öne çıkıyor.
Bloomberg'ün paylaştığı bilgilere göre Nvidia, yalnızca 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğinde Çin'e yaklaşık 2,4 milyar dolarlık Hopper mimarili veri merkezi ürünü sattı. Jensen Huang, ABD'nin gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerinin Çin'e satışını kısıtlayan politikalarına uzun süredir karşı çıkıyordu. Huang, Çin pazarını tamamen yerel üreticilere bırakmanın ABD teknoloji sektörü açısından olumsuz sonuçlar doğurabileceğini savunuyordu. Nvidia'nın yeni yönetimi altında alınan son karar ise şirketin bu yaklaşımından uzaklaşmaya başladığına işaret ediyor.
Nvidia'nın kararı, ABD'nin Çin'in gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerine erişimini sınırlamak amacıyla getirdiği yeni düzenlemelerle aynı döneme denk geliyor. ABD Ticaret Bakanlığı'nın açıkladığı yeni kurallar , Çinli şirketlerin yurt dışındaki veri merkezleri üzerinden gelişmiş ABD çiplerinden yararlanmasını da zorlaştırıyor. Düzenleme kapsamında, Çinli şirketlere belirli bir seviyenin üzerinde işlem gücü sağlayan yabancı veri merkezlerine gelişmiş çip gönderilmesi için ABD'den lisans alınması gerekiyor.
Paylaşılan bilgilere göre; yatırım bankası Jefferies, söz konusu ihracat kurallarının gelecek yıl Nvidia'nın veri merkezi gelirlerinde 44 ila 62 milyar dolar arasında kayba yol açabileceğini tahmin ediyor. Colette Kress ise Vera Rubin gibi yeni nesil Nvidia ürünlerine yönelik güçlü talebin bu kaybın şirketin toplam gelirlerine yansımasını engelleyebileceğini belirtiyor.
Yeni düzenlemelerin uzun vadede Singapur, Malezya, Tayland ve Endonezya gibi ülkelerdeki Nvidia müşterilerini de etkilemesi bekleniyor. Çin'den gelen talebin Nvidia'nın toplam gelirlerinin yüzde 20'sine kadarını oluşturabileceği tahmin ediliyor.
Öte yandan Çin yönetiminin, Nvidia'nın kararından önce de H200 çiplerinin ülkeye girişine sıcak bakmadığı belirtiliyor. Çin, özellikle Huawei gibi yerli üreticilerin geliştirdiği yapay zeka çiplerinin kullanımını artırmayı hedefliyor. Buna rağmen ülkedeki büyük yapay zeka şirketleri, Nvidia'nın gelişmiş çiplerini kullanmaya devam etmek istiyor.
Nvidia'nın H200 satışlarını sonlandırması, Jensen Huang'ın ayrılışının ardından şirketin Çin politikasındaki ilk önemli değişikliklerden biri olarak öne çıkıyor. Yeni ihracat kuralları da göz önüne alındığında, Nvidia'nın önümüzdeki dönemde Çin'e bağlı gelirlerini azaltarak farklı pazarlara ve yeni nesil ürünlere daha fazla ağırlık vermesi beklenebilir.

The ICJ rules on The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar. Here’s what’s at stake for the Rohingya.
On Thursday, November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its verdict in a landmark case brought by The Gambia, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority.
The ruling, which will be final and cannot be appealed, comes seven years after The Gambia filed its case with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and more than nine years after a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority who have lived for centuries in Rakhine State, western Myanmar.
Successive governments, from military rule under General Ne Win (1962 to 1988), to the civilian-led administration of Aung San Suu Kyi (2016 to 2021), have consistently treated them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh, while a 1982 citizenship law left most of them stateless.
They have faced repeated waves of violence and displacement, but the crisis came to a head in August 2017.
When fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) – a rebel group – attacked police posts, the military launched what it called “clearance operations” across northern Rakhine.
Survivors described massacres, rapes and entire villages burned to the ground, and more than 740,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh within months.
In November 2019, The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ, arguing that it had breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.
At the time, Myanmar was led by Aung San Suu Kyi’s civilian government, but the military, under commander-in-chief Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, controlled the security forces which carried out the crackdown.
Min Aung Hlaing’s military government then came to power in a 2021 coup and has defended the case at the ICJ.
Myanmar denies the charge, saying its forces were responding to armed attacks.
Unlike in a criminal trial, the ICJ does not judge individuals. It asks whether Myanmar as a state is responsible for genocide, and what it must do to make amends.
Today, about 520,000 Rohingya remain in Myanmar, many living under severe restrictions, while about 1.2 million are refugees in Bangladesh.
They are widely dispersed, with most still unable to return to their homes.
Nearly nine years after the 2017 exodus, about 1.2 million Rohingya are still living in Bangladesh, mostly in the crowded refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar.
Bangladesh, which wants them to return to Myanmar, restricts their movement and limits their access to formal work, leaving families heavily dependent on aid .
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of deepening insecurity and fewer long-term solutions, made worse by cuts to life-saving aid.
Shortly after US President Donald Trump commenced his second term in the White House in 2025, his administration froze or cut much of the country’s foreign aid, disrupting aid programmes in Bangladesh. Other countries have also cut foreign aid spending as costs elsewhere have risen in recent years.
A UNHCR study found that these cuts have weakened services for refugees such as registration, legal aid, healthcare, education and child protection, exposing refugees to greater risks of trafficking, forced labour and child marriage.
For the roughly 520,000 Rohingya still in Myanmar since the 2017 crackdown, conditions have worsened since the country’s 2021 military coup.
The Arakan Army, a rebel group fighting for autonomy for Rakhine, now controls most of Rakhine State. It has been accused of seizing land, arbitrary killings and torture, while the military has forcibly conscripted Rohingya men to fight against it.
In August 2024, hundreds of Rohingya fleeing fighting in Maungdaw were reportedly killed by drone and artillery strikes while crossing the Naf River into Bangladesh.
Su Mon, Asia Pacific senior analyst at ACLED , said: “These conditions prevent any safe, voluntary, or dignified return of Rohingya refugees. All communities in Rakhine State face severe food insecurity, lack of aid, an economic collapse, and relentless conflict.”
With little hope at home or in the camps, thousands have been boarding boats to Malaysia and Indonesia each year.
The UNHCR estimates 3,135 people have died or gone missing at sea since 2022, while 2025 was the deadliest year on record, with 900 lives lost.
The Gambia , a small Muslim-majority country in West Africa, has no direct connection to the violence in Myanmar. It brought the case on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), of which it is an active member.
Some observers also link The Gambia’s position to its own history. As the Rohingya crisis unfolded, the country was investigating killings and abductions committed under former leader Yahya Jammeh, who ruled for 22 years until 2017.
The Gambia accuses Myanmar’s military of killing Rohingya, causing physical and mental harm, imposing conditions designed to destroy the group and preventing births during its so-called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine.
It also described widespread sexual violence, which it alleges is a central part of this campaign.
Myanmar says its operations targeted Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) fighters and their supporters, accusing The Gambia of downplaying the threat they posed.
The key question the court has examined is whether Myanmar intended to destroy the Rohingya as a group, a requirement for proving genocide.
The Gambia points to the brutality of the attacks, official tolerance of hate speech and the failure to investigate abuses as evidence of that intent.
Myanmar says there is no direct evidence of such intent and that The Gambia has failed to prove it.
The Gambia is asking the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to ensure the Rohingya can safely return home. Other demands include restoring their property, recognising their right to identify as Rohingya and providing compensation where property cannot be returned.
Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on behalf of Rohingya victims.
The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed, and Myanmar is legally bound to follow it. But the ICJ has no way to enforce its decisions.
If Myanmar ignores the ruling, The Gambia can ask the UN Security Council to act. The council has never used this power and any of its five permanent members could block action with a veto. China and Russia have shielded Myanmar there before.
Other countries and the UN General Assembly can also apply political pressure on Myanmar to comply.
The court could also stop short of a genocide finding. In 2007, it ruled that Serbia had not committed genocide in Bosnia, but had failed to prevent the Srebrenica massacre .
The ICJ has rarely found a state responsible for genocide, largely because proving intent to destroy a group is very difficult.
In 2007, the court ruled that Serbia was not directly responsible for committing genocide in Bosnia. However, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed.
How judges apply this high legal threshold in the Myanmar case will be closely watched, particularly for what it could mean for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over Gaza.

Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were banned for their part in the sandpaper plot
Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian, , external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught
Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".
Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."
'No way in a million years' the whole team didn't know - Vaughan on sandpaper scandal
Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."
Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.
In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.
"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.
"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."
In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".
In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.
"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."
For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.
Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.
His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.
In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.
Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.
It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.
But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named name…

Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.
No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.
"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.
Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".
Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.
The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning .
Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.
When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.
"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.
The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.
Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.
And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
The leaders of China , the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine .
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran .
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

Economists predict GTA 6 could cost US up to $1bn in lost productivity, with the game set for release at midnight.
It’s taken more than a decade and is estimated to have cost upwards of $1bn, but arguably the most anticipated release in gaming history is finally here.
Depending on where you live, Grand Theft Auto VI , better known as GTA 6, is now available to play. Digital intelligence company Sensor Tower estimates that Rockstar Games has already generated about $1.1bn in pre-order revenue, making it the largest pre-order launch in history.
So, what can gamers expect? And, more importantly, will it live up to the hype?
The latest instalment in the hugely popular franchise will be released across all regions at midnight local time tonight, Rockstar Games has confirmed. Those who have pre-ordered the game can already download it, allowing them to start playing GTA 6 as soon as the clock strikes 12am.
The action-adventure game will be available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. Gamers will also be able to play it on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming.
Depending on the console you own, you’ll need up to 212GB of free storage space to download GTA 6. The process could take several hours, depending on your internet speed. Connecting your console directly to your router using an Ethernet cable could significantly reduce download times.
Video games have come a long way since the turn of the century, and so has GTA. The franchise has become the crown jewel of an industry that generated more than $201bn for the global economy in 2025, according to Newzoo.
In short, GTA is a cash cow, and its fans believe the profits are well-deserved. Reports suggest that GTA V Online, the previous instalment in the series, still generates an average of $1.3m a day for Rockstar Games.
GTA 6, like its predecessor, will feature more than one main protagonist. The game is set in the fictional Vice City, based on Miami, Florida.
The story centres on lovers and criminals Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose lives resemble those of the notorious crime couple Bonnie and Clyde. The pair were gunned down by US law enforcement in 1934 during an ambush, after more than two years of robbing banks and killing police officers.
GTA 6 is set to feature even more crime and violence than previous editions, with the main story reportedly taking about 50 hours to complete. Meanwhile, achieving 100 percent completion could take as long as 200 hours.
The map is expected to be roughly twice the size of GTA V’s, with hundreds of enterable buildings, more than 170 animal species and enhanced artificial intelligence (AI), making it potentially the most realistic instalment in the franchise to date.
The wanted system, which is usually triggered when players commit crimes, has also been revamped. Players will be able to reach a wanted level of six stars for the most serious offences, while lesser crimes could attract as little as one star.
In a game where breaking the law is as normal as washing your face, Rockstar Games has focused on replicating the investigative processes used by real-life police. Computer-controlled characters, commonly known as non-playable characters (NPCs), will now be able to alert the police when they witness a crime.
Security cameras will also be able to capture Jason and Lucia, providing officers with additional intelligence. That means you’ll have to work harder to get the police off your tail. Officers will gather several clues about your misdeeds, forcing players to take multiple steps to avoid getting caught, including changing their appearance and switching vehicles.
Employers around the world could face staffing difficulties tomorrow. Opinium, a market research agency, estimates that 4.1 million working days in the United Kingdom alone could be lost due to employees calling in sick so they can spend the day playing GTA 6.
Those who are more organised have booked the big day off in advance, including Karl O’Connor, 34, who lives in Watford, a town just outside northwest London. O’Connor works full-time as a cinema manager and says that Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, is his favourite video game ever.
“I was 10 years old when it was released,” he told Al Jazeera.
“It was very formative in the way I consume art. I was falling in love with music around this time and the [game] soundtrack accelerated that by expanding on the range of genres I enjoy. I have tomorrow off and have used my last day of annual leave to extend my two days off next week to three.”
O’Connor isn’t alone. Andy Baker, 33, lives in Belfast, Northern Ireland. Baker works as a courier and will finish work Wednesday at 4pm local time and won’t return until Sunday.
“I’m trying not to get too excited in case it’s [the game] a letdown but realistically it shouldn’t be as the money they’ve spent is crazy.”
Baker said he’s “staying away” from social media to avoid any spoilers.
Tech giant Logitech has already priced in the productivity loss and has given all of its 7,000 employees a paid day off to play the game free of guilt.
“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” Hanneke Faber, Logitech’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”
According to reports, some economists predict GTA 6 could cost the US economy as much as $1bn in lost productivity. Rockstar Games won’t lose any sleep, however, with analysts expecting the company to make up to $5bn in global sales in just the first week of the release.

Haiti announced on Tuesday that it formalised a "cooperation agreement" with El Salvador, the same day thousands of Haitians showed support in the streets of Port-au-Prince for soldiers sent by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs in the capital.
"The Council of Ministers has approved the Cooperation agreement between the Republic of Haiti and the Republic of El Salvador," according to a Facebook post from the Haitian executive, who called it "a new stage in strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation."
Signs carried by the demonstrators on Tuesday read "Thank you, Bukele," and "Long live Bukele," according to photographs taken by an AFP journalist.
"Bukele, the country belongs to you! Do whatever you want with it," some chanted in the streets of a capital long subsumed by gang violence that has seized control of large sections.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from his country went missing during an operation of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The new Salvadoran deployment, despite being separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought reinforcements.
"We are asking President Bukele to ignore the detractors and to continue supporting Haiti," a demonstrator who declined to be identified for security reasons told AFP.
Numerous armed forces are now operating in Haiti, with uncertain levels of coordination, including the Haitian police and army, the multinational GSF, foreign mercenaries and most recently, the Salvadoran soldiers.
Bukele, whose forceful gang crackdown at home has won public support but sparked accusations of rights violations, appears prepared for more than just finding the four lost soldiers.
On 10 November, he boasted of having destroyed the "headquarters" of one of Haiti's main gangs, accompanied by video footage of the helicopter attack.
Since then, Bukele's forces have taken over a football stadium in the capital with the support of Haiti's national police.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called on all security forces to protect the population and resort to lethal force only as a last resort.
In the first 10 months of 2026, the UN recorded 4,595 deaths and 2,050 injuries to armed violence in Haiti.
In Miami over the weekend, at a football match between Haiti and the United States, some Haitian fans cheered on both their national team and Bukele, expressing high hopes the island's gangs can be contained.
Despite the 6-0 loss to the US in the Concacaf Nations League match, Haitians expressed optimism, waving Salvadoran flags and shouting "Bukele! Bukele!"
"All I can say is 'Viva Bukele!'," said 41-year-old Haitian fan Guito Ledix, adding that Bukele "is the only one trying to see if there's any possibility of getting rid of the gangs."
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deep political and security crisis for years, with gangs seizing control of the island nation through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.
From Miami, home to one of the largest concentrations of Haitian immigrants, 28-year-old Stephanie Jeanty frets about the safety of her family still living there.
"Before I was a bit more stressed, but now, seeing the Salvadoran delegation that is working to restore peace, it's something, things are better," she said.
"I would really like to go back to my country. For now, no."

PRESS REVIEW – Wednesday, November 18: A joint investigation following the leak of 15 million documents shows that Deutsche Bank turned a blind eye to the criminal activities of some of its clients. Next, for its 175th birthday, The New York Times has chosen the top 10 stories that made history. Wired is focusing on the moments that defined 2026. Finally, we bring you a story about American parents whose children dream of becoming Formula 1 drivers. But how much does that dream cost?
The Financial Times reports that in 2018, when CEO Christian Sewing took over at Deutsche Bank, he promised to put an end to scandals and clean up the bank. Eight years later, the reality is quite different. The British daily investigated the leak of 15 million documents in collaboration with several international media outlets, including Le Monde and Der Spiegel . The Financial Times says the documents expose "bad behaviour, systemic failures, incompetence and broken promises". The leak and the reporting throw a new light on the career of the chief executive and his double standards. Der Spiegel writes about Deutsche Bank's "dark secrets". It points out that when Sewing took over, the institution had already been accused of various shortcomings, including money laundering . The bank had already been the subject of at least 27 raids and had received fines and sanctions totalling more than €20 billion since the beginning of the 2000s.
The bank is also under fire for its ties to Russian oligarchs and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . Der Spiegel specifically names several Russian oligarchs subject to sanctions, as well as Epstein. The German magazine reports that the late paedophile became a client of Deutsche Bank in 2013 – well after his conviction in 2008 – a conviction which Deutsche Bank was fully aware of. The sexual predator carried out his transactions there, totalling more than half a billion dollars, until 2019. The bank finally stopped working with Epstein three days after his arrest. Le Monde looks at the bank's links with another famous – or infamous – American: US President Donald Trump . An internal investigation established "a formal and direct link" between at least one of Trump's companies and money-laundering operations in Azerbaijan . Deutsche Bank knew this but didn't sever its ties with the US president – it just reinforced confidentiality, protecting both Trump and itself.
Next, it's The New York Times 's 175th birthday. For the occasion, the paper has chosen the 10 days that changed the world since the paper started publishing. For example, "The Day God Was Dethroned" – on November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published "On the Origin of Species" and changed how people see their place in the universe; "The Day We Saw Our End" – on August 6, 1945, the United States bombed Hiroshima with the atomic bomb; and "The Day That Rewired Us" – on October 29, 1969, the first message on the ARPANET network was sent, the ancestor of the internet as we know it today.
Wired Magazine is focusing on 2026 in its "inaugural yearbook". It celebrates the people, inventions and viral moments that defined this year. Andy Burnham has said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw her “crass and insensitive” comment justifying cuts to disability benefits on the grounds that “double amputees run marathons”.
After Badenoch used this line in a speech last week , the Paralympian Richard Whitehead posted a message on Facebook criticising her. He said:
double quotation mark Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day.
The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary. Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance.
In subsequent remarks, Whitehead said that Badenoch’s comments were “divisive” and that he was “gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way”.
At PMQs today, the Labour MP Charlotte Nichols asked Burnham whether he agreed with Whitehead that “the achievements of our sports men and women with disabilities should never be weaponised against others”.
double quotation mark I thought the comments by Richard Whitehead do deserve a response from the right honourable lady [Badenoch]. They were crass and insensitive, and I think she should withdraw them.
Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals.
Guardian readers probably don’t need much persuading that PMQs is a terrible forum for reasonable debate, and there was a good example today that shows why. In his final response to Kemi Badenoch, Burnham accused her of adopting a “patronising tone”. This was uncharacteristically personal, and it lit up on social media as about the most interesting line from the exchange, with some commentators implying it was a gaffe. In reality, of course, it was probably one of the least contentious things Burnham said. Badenoch is patronising, particularly at PMQs. If there were a world championships for being patronising, she would be leading the UK team. Yet Burnham will probably conclude that it was a mistake, and something he shouldn’t have said.
Why? Because it made him look a bit rattled. Burnham came into office determined to pursue “problem solving, not point scoring”, but increasingly that is looking like a lost cause and the centrifugal power of PMQs yanks him back into a slanging match. (He is not always like this with opposition backbenchers, but he is – inevitably – with Badenoch.) Today, speaking to the Tory leader, he seemed to devote more time than ever to attacking her party’s record, rather than seeking common ground. On the plus side, the points he was making about the Conservatives’ record, and about her policy agenda now consisting of little more than welfare cuts, were forceful. On the negative side, he sounded like someone on the defensive.
Just as she did last week, Badenoch was reasonably good at delivering the sort of broad-brush ‘You’re rubbish’ messaging that would work as a headline for a Daily Express op ed. But it was hard to discern what particular attack line she wanted to land. There was a time when she would arrive at PMQs with a pre-prepared gotcha question and afterwards, normally following Keir Starmer’s refusal to answer, CCHQ would send out a press release highlighting the alleged implications of the question-dodging. There was none of that today, or last week.
One of Badenoch’s most interesting claims was that Burnham is just offering the “vibes” of welfare reform, not the real thing. But that claim is so wide of the mark it is unlikely to work even with a Tory audience. The Milburn plan may have its drawbacks, but it is absurd to dismiss it as just vibes.
Sky News also set Badenoch up for another attack, highlighting Alan Milburn saying yesterday that some people would lose from the reforms, while Burnham said in a separate interview he did not want anyone to lose out. It was a classic case of apples and pears; Milburn was saying people will lose out from the benefit cuts, while Burnham was saying that, because those cuts are part of a strategy intended to divert off benefits into work, in the long run they wouldn’t lose out. Mindful, perhaps, of the ‘if you’re explaining, you’re losing’ theory of political communications, Burnham did not want to clarify this, and he just sidestepped her question. Badenoch then did not pursue the point, which was strange because a follow-up question could have made it much more awkward for him.

Haitians take to the streets to praise El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and his soldiers for fighting gangs in the country.
Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections of the capital.
Protesters on Tuesday carried signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele”.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from El Salvador went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The latest Salvadoran deployment, although separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought additional reinforcements to combat the gangs.
Bukele’s hardline crackdown on gangs in El Salvador has broad public support but has drawn accusations of human rights violations.
On November 10, he claimed to have destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs, releasing video footage of a helicopter attack.
Since then, Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have taken control of a football stadium in the capital.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to prioritise the protection of civilians and to use lethal force only as a measure of last resort.
In the first 10 months of this year, the UN recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deepening political and security crisis, with gangs tightening their grip on the country through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.

The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague .
The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.
A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.
Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.
A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.
"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]…. International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.
"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.
In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.
Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.
Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.
The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.
As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.
"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.
Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.
Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.
Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.
The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.
"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.
"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.
O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.
Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State , they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.
"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.
The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.
"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.
"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.
The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.
The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.
What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.
Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.
Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.
"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

Files show Epstein-linked payments at $582m, far more than previously known, and tie Trump business dealings to suspected money laundering networks.
A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerful figures.
The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation, published on Tuesday by a consortium of international news outlets, has put Germany’s biggest bank back in the spotlight after years of trying to rebuild its reputation following its failures to prevent money laundering.
Files containing millions of emails, minutes of meetings and internal reports were leaked by two whistleblowers whose identities and links to the institution have been withheld for their protection, according to Le Monde, one of the participating news outlets. The pair told the media groups they believed the bank was engaging in criminal activity and that releasing the documents was in the public interest.
Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife obtained the cache, which they then shared with more than 230 reporters from about 50 news organisations, including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and The New York Times, in an internationally coordinated effort.
The material includes some nine million emails, as well as meeting minutes, due diligence reports and financial crime reports dating back to the early 2010s, many of them from the bank’s internal investigations.
The whistleblowers also passed the data to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities, and could be eligible for a reward if Washington prosecutes the bank based on their leaks. Le Monde said the whistleblowers were not paid by the journalists and placed no conditions on how the material was used.
Deutsche Bank said concerns raised by the investigation “date back many years” and that it had since strengthened its controls, adding that it did not expect any meaningful financial impact. The bank’s chairman reaffirmed the board’s support for chief executive Christian Sewing, who has run the institution since 2018.
“Deutsche Bank is a different bank today,” the bank said in a statement.
The files identify more than $3m in transactions involving Trump-owned companies, including payments linked to suspected Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks.
Deutsche Bank extended loans to Trump for years, even after a string of bankruptcies and defaults at his businesses from the early 1990s. By January 2021, it was his biggest creditor, with about $340m in loans to his company outstanding.
That month, following the January 6 assault on the US Capitol by protesters wanting to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s win in the presidential election, the bank ceased doing business with him, according to The New York Times. Trump had claimed the election had been rigged against him, of which there has never been any proof.
The Financial Times reported that the bank inadvertently sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term in office, and never told him about the error. Asked about the disclosure during his visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit on Tuesday, Trump said the bank should not have released that information.
“They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his remarks.
The leaked records also reveal special monitoring that the bank applied to Trump’s accounts, and its handling of them has drawn scrutiny before.
In 2019, The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank had failed to alert US authorities to suspicious transactions linked to Trump. The bank said at the time that none of its investigators had been prevented from escalating such concerns.
The leaked files list about $582m in transactions linked to Epstein, which were flagged internally as suspicious. That is more than double the amount previously identified as being overlooked or not reported by banks during US Senate investigations . When the Senate findings were released in August, a Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank regretted its “historical connection” with Epstein.
Epstein, who was a US financier, became a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, and remained a client until 2018. He died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
Internal emails in the newly leaked cache indicate that senior executives approved Epstein as a client despite his conviction, and kept his accounts open even after warnings about the activities of Ghislaine Maxwell, his former girlfriend and associate. Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein sexually abuse teenage girls. She is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The files also reveal information about payments linked to wealthy Epstein associates such as private equity billionaire Leon Black and Wall Street financier Glenn Dubin.
A review commissioned by Black’s firm previously found he had paid Epstein $158m between 2012 and 2017 for tax and estate planning advice. Black has sought to distance himself from Epstein, repeatedly denying wrongdoing or any knowledge of his abuse of girls and young women.
The leak comes years after the bank paid fines and settlements of more than $200m over its handling of Epstein-related finances. In 2020, regulators fined it $150m for compliance failures linked to Epstein and other high-risk clients, finding that he had held more than 40 accounts at the bank. In 2023, it agreed to pay $75m to settle a suit brought by women who alleged they had been abused by him.
The documents also detail Deutsche Bank’s business dealings in Russia up until Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite concerns raised by some managers.
They include previously undisclosed internal warnings about the bank’s continued dealings with wealthy Kremlin-connected clients despite sanctions and money laundering concerns.
Those named include Russian billionaires Roman Abramovich, the former owner of English football club Chelsea, and aluminium tycoon Oleg Deripaska. Both men were sanctioned by the United Kingdom in 2022. Suleiman Kerimov, another billionaire whose name appears in the files, was sanctioned by the US in 2014 and 2018.
Transactions associated with Rifaat al-Assad , the uncle of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, also appear in the files. Rifaat, who died in January, was convicted in France in 2020 of acquiring millions of euros’ worth of property with funds diverted from the Syrian state.
Other files concern figures connected to the Sarkozy-Libya affair, in which former French President Nicolas Sarkozy was convicted in 2025 of criminal conspiracy over efforts to secure funding for his 2007 campaign from the government of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

Britannia Global Markets'tan Neil Welsh, fiyatın 3 bin 800 dolara inebileceğini, bunun iki yıllık yükselişin yüzde 50'lik düzeltme seviyesi olduğunu söylemişti. Carsten Fritsch ise borsa yatırım fonlarından (ETF) gelecek satışların fiyatları daha da aşağı çekebileceği uyarısında bulundu.
Alberto Musalem, enflasyonu kontrol altına almak için Fed'in birkaç faiz artırımına ihtiyaç duyabileceğini belirtti. Piyasalar bu cümleyi, faiz patikasının daha önce fiyatlanandan yukarıda seyredeceği şeklinde okudu.
Sıkı para politikası beklentisi dolar tarafını güçlendiriyor. Faiz getirisi olmayan altın ise yükselen dolar ve yükselen faiz ortamında yatırımcının gözünden hızla düşüyor. Kitco'ya göre geçen hafta bazı Fed yetkilileri, gelecek ay yapılabilecek 50 baz puanlık bir artışı destekleyen yorumlar yapmıştı.
John Williams, daha fazla sıkılaştırmayı desteklediğini söylerken piyasadaki daha agresif artırım beklentisine karşı da temkinli davrandı. Yani mesaj net: artırım yolu açık ama adım büyüklüğü tartışmalı.
Fiyatlamalar da bunu yansıtıyor. Piyasalar Aralık ayında 25 baz puanlık artışı yaklaşık yüzde 96, 50 baz puanlık artışı ise yaklaşık yüzde 4 olasılıkla fiyatlıyor. LPL Financial'dan Jeffrey Roach da 25 baz puan beklediğini, 50 baz puanın gereksiz risk yaratabileceğini ifade etmişti.
Gram altın güne 6 bin 236 liradan başladı, gün içinde 6 bin 132 liraya kadar indi ve yüzde 1,57 kayıpla 6 bin 138 lira 68 kuruştan satıldı. Çeyrek altın 9 bin 951 lira, yarım altın 19 bin 902 lira, tam altın ise 39 bin 743 lira seviyesine geriledi. 14 ayar gram 3 bin 583 lira, 18 ayar gram 4 bin 592 liradan işlem gördü.
Düşüş tüm ürünlere eşit yansımadı. Cumhuriyet altını yüzde 0,04 artışla 42 bin 184 liraya, Reşat altını yine yüzde 0,04 artışla 43 bin 461 liraya çıktı. Yatırımcılar şimdi Fed'in FOMC toplantı tutanaklarını bekliyor, altının yönünü bu metinden çıkacak faiz sinyalinin belirlemesi bekleniyor.
